transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone.
Mexican authorities say they have captured one of the most wanted drug lords in the country.
NPR's Ada Peralta reports he was on the FBI's "10 Most Wanted" list.
Fausto Isidro Mesaflores, who was better known as El Chapo Isidro, is the leader of the Beltranleva cartel.
The U.S. accuses him of running huge quantities of drugs, including meth and fentanyl, to the U.S.
The Mexican military says it captured Mesaflores in Wasave, Sinaloa, using U.S. intelligence.
Residents reported that the military fired from helicopters while the cartels burned cars and trucks.
A baseball game was disrupted by the heavy fighting, and some residents had to spend the night at a supermarket to stay safe.
Over the past couple of years, as the U.S. has mounted pressure on Mexico to fight organized crime,
security forces have captured a number of drug lords.
The power vacuums have often led to an increase in violence.
Ada Peralta, NPR News, Mexico City.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie says that on guidance from the National Weather Service
and NOAA forecasting significant high tides and heavy rain,
he's encouraging people not to travel over the coming Thanksgiving week.
I know there's a lot of travel for many of you as you head into the Thanksgiving holiday,
but I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential
starting Monday afternoon and going into Wednesday afternoon.
We are expecting tides that the National Weather Service told us they have never seen before in recorded history here in San Francisco.
On the East Coast, meanwhile, a storm is forming off Florida's Atlantic shores with the potential of strengthening into a tropical or subtropical storm.
The system is expected to move north into Georgia, the Carolinas and the middle Atlantic states.
AAA is forecasting that 81.5 million people in the United States will be traveling for this holiday week.
This week, the Senate passed a bipartisan bill meant to overhaul the permitting process to build new energy projects.
As NPR's Matthew Brown reports, this could shorten or remove the environmental review processes used by federal regulators.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act could bring major changes to American infrastructure.
It could also narrow the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act.
The bill received strong bipartisan support and backing from industry groups representing renewable energy companies as well as oil and gas suppliers.
But environmental groups are pushing back.
They're concerned that the bill will mostly benefit fossil fuel projects.
And tribal organizations warn that some provisions may restrict their ability to review projects at culturally significant indigenous sites.
The bill still must pass the House before President Trump signs it.
That may not happen in the crowded final months for this Republican-led Congress.
Matthew Brown, NPR News, Washington.
This is NPR News.
President Trump is advising U.S. tech companies that if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries, they will be heavily taxed.
The president told reporters yesterday that Americans should welcome data centers in their neighborhoods.
A mathematician at Anthropics says he may have solved what's been called the holy grail of math problems with help from the company's chatbot, Claude.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports the Riemann hypothesis has been an open question for more than 160 years.
Rutgers University mathematician Alex Contruvic says he never expected to see a proof of the Riemann hypothesis in his lifetime.
I thought I was done picking myself up off the floor.
And I'm shocked. And I'm still shocked.
The hypothesis describes how prime numbers are spread out, and getting to a solution means drawing on decades of work across different branches of mathematics.
The new claim involves just massive, massive amounts of mathematics.
There's no human being that has all of that in their head.
Teams of human mathematicians will now examine parts of the computer code and piece together how the proof works.
Contruvic says understanding the proposed proof from Anthropic could take months.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
The president's plans for a triumphal arch have now been blocked by a second federal judge.
The second ruling in Virginia keeps action on the plans at bay.
As consideration continues through multiple lawsuits, a county board in Virginia called it a public safety risk in a traffic obstruction.
I'm Louise Givoni, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Mexican military captures drug lord Fausto Isidro Mesaflores, leader of Beltranleva cartel, in Sinaloa
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie urges residents to avoid non-essential travel over Thanksgiving week due to tides
Storm forming off Florida's Atlantic coast could strengthen into tropical or subtropical storm
AAA forecasts 81.5 million Americans will travel during Thanksgiving holiday week
Senate passes bipartisan bill overhauling energy project permitting and narrowing environmental reviews
Trump warns tech companies building AI data centers abroad will face heavy taxes
Anthropic mathematician claims proof of Riemann hypothesis with help from Claude chatbot
Federal judge in Virginia blocks Trump's triumphal arch plans, a second such ruling
